q: Why is there no animal that is good at everything?
Why is a universally optimal animal impossible rather than merely absent?
What excludes a universally optimal phenotype?
options: Because getting better at one thing makes you worse at another
Because it would be too expensive to grow
Because they would take over the world
why: Armour is heavy, so it slows you down. Big muscles need lots of food. Being small means you cannot be strong. You cannot have all of it because the things fight each other.

Traits compete for a shared budget and some are physically contradictory. Armour adds the mass that speed requires you not to carry; large muscles require the food supply that small size exists to avoid needing.

Two separate mechanisms, and both are needed for the full argument. Shared resource budgets make simultaneous maximisation costly; physical contradiction makes it impossible. Only the second explains the complete absence rather than the rarity.

q: Why does a mouse have to eat so much for its size?
Why is mass-specific metabolic rate higher in small animals?
Why does the square-cube law force high mass-specific metabolism at small size?
options: It has much more outside for its inside, so heat pours out
Mice are greedy
Small animals have bigger stomachs for their size
why: Heat is made by the inside and lost through the outside. A small animal has loads of outside for very little inside, so it loses heat fast and has to keep replacing it — which means eating almost all the time.

Heat production scales with volume and heat loss with surface, so as size falls the loss term grows relative to the production term. The animal compensates by running its metabolism faster, and pays for it by needing to eat almost continuously.

It is a ratio problem rather than an absolute one. A shrew loses less heat in total than an elephant and vastly more per gram, and it is the per-gram figure that determines how hard the metabolism has to work. Kleiber's exponent of 0.75 sits between the 0.67 of pure surface scaling and the 1.0 of pure volume scaling, which is itself informative.

q: Why is swimming the cheapest way to travel?
Why is the energy cost per distance lowest for swimming?
Why does swimming have the lowest cost of transport?
options: The water holds you up, so no energy goes into not falling
Water is thinner than air
Swimming animals are lazier
why: A running animal spends energy holding itself up and lifting itself with every step. A fish is already held up by the water, so all its effort goes into going forwards.

Buoyancy removes the cost of supporting body weight, which is a large part of what walking and running spend energy on. Everything left goes into overcoming drag — so per kilometre, swimming wins comfortably despite water being far denser than air.

Cost of transport separates into supporting weight and overcoming resistance. Buoyancy nearly eliminates the first term, and although drag in water is much higher than in air, the elimination outweighs it at the speeds animals actually use. Flight is the opposite case: it must pay for support continuously, which is why it is the most expensive per unit time and yet efficient per unit distance.

q: Can natural selection change how an animal behaves?
Can behaviour evolve by natural selection?
Why does the mechanism apply to behaviour without modification?
options: Yes — behaviour is inherited, so the same three conditions apply
No, selection only changes bodies
Only if the animal practises
why: The three conditions are about differences being passed on and mattering for survival. They never say the difference has to be a colour or a bone. If a behaviour is inherited and it matters, it gets selected.

Nothing in the mechanism refers to the physical nature of the trait. Behaviour varies, is heritable, and affects survival and reproduction, so it satisfies all three conditions and is selected on identically.

The mechanism is substrate-neutral, which is why it also describes antibiotic resistance and clonal selection in your immune system. That generality is the strongest thing about it — and it is why 'evolution of behaviour' needs no separate theory.

q: Why is a short parts list not a problem?
Why does a small monomer set not limit variety?
Why is monomer diversity not the binding constraint?
options: Because the order they are joined in does the work
Because the pieces are very complicated
Because living things are all quite similar
why: Twenty different beads on a string a hundred beads long gives more orders than there are atoms in the universe. The pieces do not need to be clever.
Variety comes from sequence, not from inventory. Twenty amino acids in a chain of 100 gives 20¹⁰⁰ possible proteins — a number with 130 digits, against roughly 10⁸⁰ atoms in the observable universe.

This is the same argument as the four-letter alphabet in DNA, and it generalises: capacity scales exponentially with length and only linearly with alphabet size, so the interesting constraints are always on length, error rate and assembly cost rather than on the parts list.

q: Why does sugar not release its energy on its own?
Why is glucose stable in a bowl but not in a cell?
Why is glucose kinetically stable despite being thermodynamically unstable?
options: It needs something to start it off and take it apart
It has no energy until you eat it
Sugar only works inside a body
why: The energy is there the whole time. It just needs something to get it started — which is exactly why a sugar cube burns if you light it, and does nothing if you do not.
Releasing the energy requires getting over a barrier first. Heat does it crudely; an enzyme does it at body temperature, in small steps, capturing the energy instead of losing it.

The reaction is strongly favourable and extremely slow, which is the definition of kinetic stability. Enzymes lower the activation barrier without altering ΔG, so they change the rate and never the yield — the same amount of energy is available whether it is burnt or respired.

q: What actually pushes oil into a blob?
Where does the driving force for hydrophobic association come from?
Why is the hydrophobic effect not an attraction between oily molecules?
options: The water, getting itself out of the way
The oil molecules gripping each other
Gravity
why: Oily things are not sticky. Water is just much happier next to other water, so it shoves the oil together to get on with it.

The force comes from the solvent. Water has to arrange itself into a rigid cage around an exposed oily surface; shrinking that surface releases the cage, and that release is what drives the association.

The effect is entropic and lives in the water, not enthalpic and living in the oil. The clearest evidence is the temperature dependence: over a broad range hydrophobic association gets stronger as you warm it, which no ordinary attraction between two molecules does.

q: Why does changing one bead matter so much?
Why can a single substitution abolish function?
Why is the sequence-structure map so unforgiving at some positions and not others?
options: Because the shape depends on the whole order at once
Because one bead is much bigger than the others
Because there are only twenty to choose from
why: The shape comes from all the beads together. Move one and the folding can come out completely different — or leave a sticky bit on the outside where there should not be one.

The fold is a global property of the sequence, so a local change can have a non-local effect. A substitution buried in the core, or one that exposes an oily surface, can wreck the structure; the same change elsewhere may do nothing at all.

Positional sensitivity varies enormously and predictably: buried core residues and active-site residues are highly constrained, surface loops are largely tolerant. This is why conservation across species is such a good predictor of which mutations will be pathogenic — evolution has already run the experiment.

q: How big is a cell?
Roughly how big is a typical human cell?
What is the approximate diameter of a typical human cell?
Order of magnitude for a typical eukaryotic cell diameter?
options: Too small to see without a microscope
About the size of a grain of sand
Big enough to see if you look closely
why: About 25 cells fit across a full stop. Your eyes stop working long before that.
About 25 fit across a full stop — roughly 20 micrometres each. The eye can just about resolve 100 micrometres, so a cell is about five times too small.
≈20 µm. Unaided visual acuity bottoms out around 100 µm, so a cell is about five times below the limit.
≈20 µm, against an unaided resolution limit near 100 µm — hence the entire history of the field waiting on lens grinding.

q: What makes a cell like a city?
Why is a cell more like a city than like a brick?
In what sense is a cell a system rather than a component?
Why does the city analogy hold and the brick analogy fail?
options: It has many parts, each doing a different job
It is made of one solid material
It is the same all the way through
why: A brick is the same all the way through. A cell has power, walls and instructions — all different, all working at once.
A brick is uniform. A cell has a boundary, power plants, an instruction store and transport, all running at the same time and depending on each other.
A brick is homogeneous and passive. A cell is compartmentalised and active: each organelle performs a distinct function, and removing one stops the whole.
The analogy holds on functional differentiation and interdependence — remove the power plant and the instruction store stops being read. A brick has neither property.

q: Why did the poison stay outside?
Why did the poison stay out when the food got in?
What determined which molecules crossed the membrane?
What is the selectivity mechanism at work here?
options: It was too big for the holes
The cell pushed it away
Poison cannot move
why: The holes were big enough for food and too small for poison. Nothing pushed anything — the size did all the work.
Passage depended only on size against hole size. The cell did nothing active: the food fitted and the poison did not.
Steric exclusion. Molecules smaller than the pore crossed by random motion; larger ones bounced. No energy was expended by the cell.
Steric exclusion alone. Both species executed the same unbiased random walk; only the pore geometry differed in outcome.

q: What made the food move inside?
What made the food end up inside the cell?
What drove net movement of food into the cell?
What accounts for the net inward flux of food?
options: It moved randomly and there was more room inside
The cell sucked it in
Food always moves towards cells
why: Every molecule wandered at random. There were more outside than inside, so more wandered in than out — until it evened up.
Each molecule moves randomly with no sense of direction. Because there were more outside, more happened to cross inwards than outwards, and it stopped when both sides matched.
Random motion plus a concentration difference. Flux is proportional to the gradient, so it falls to zero at equilibrium — nothing 'pulls'.
Fick's first law falling out of an unbiased random walk: net flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, and vanishes at equilibrium.

q: Why does the energy bar never stay still?
Why did the energy level never sit still, even when it was working?
Why is ATP level always changing even at steady state?
Why is a constant ATP pool not evidence of a static system?
options: Because energy is being made and spent all the time
Because the cell stores energy up
Because the sliders were moving
why: The cell never fills up. It makes energy and spends it at the same time, all the time.
There is no tank. Production and consumption run simultaneously, so the level is always the difference between two flows.
Steady state is a balance of two large opposing fluxes, not the absence of change. Stop synthesis and the pool is gone in seconds.
A constant pool reflects matched synthesis and hydrolysis rates, both large. Turnover, not stock, is the quantity that matters.

q: Why is building loads of power plants a bad idea?
Why did adding more and more power plants stop helping?
Why does mitochondrial number have an optimum rather than a maximum?
What sets the upper bound on useful mitochondrial density?
options: Each one costs energy to run
They get in each other's way
There is not enough room
why: Every power plant needs energy just to keep going. Build too many and they eat more than they make.
Each mitochondrion has a maintenance cost. Past a point, the upkeep of the extras exceeds what they contribute.
Maintenance cost scales with number while output is capped by substrate supply, so net gain turns negative — cells regulate density rather than maximising it.
Output saturates at substrate limitation while maintenance scales linearly, so net ATP is non-monotonic in copy number.

q: Why does the original stay in its room?
Why does DNA never leave the nucleus?
Why is the template retained rather than exported?
What is the functional argument for sequestering the template?
options: So it cannot be damaged or lost
Because it is stuck
Because copies are faster
why: There is only one original. If it were damaged, every copy after it would be wrong too.
You have one copy of your genome per cell. Damage to it is permanent and inherited by every daughter cell; damage to a transcript costs nothing.
The template is irreplaceable and its errors propagate; transcripts are disposable and their errors do not. Sequestering the template also allows expression to be regulated at the point of copying.
Error in a transcript is transient; error in the template is heritable. Compartmentalisation also creates a regulatory step between archive and product.

q: How does a cell know what to become?
What determines a cell's fate during development?
What is the source of positional information?
options: From where it is and what is next to it
It reads a plan of the whole body
It is decided randomly
why: There is no plan of you anywhere. A cell can only tell what is right next to it, and that turns out to be enough.
Fate follows position, and position is read from local signals — chemicals reaching the cell and contact with neighbours. No cell has access to any description of the whole.

Positional information is encoded in gradients and contacts, both strictly local. The remarkable part is that purely local rules produce a reproducible global arrangement, which is why development is the best worked example of emergence in biology.

q: How does one chemical make five different fingers?
How does a single morphogen specify multiple distinct fates?
How does a smooth gradient produce discrete boundaries?
options: Different amounts mean different things
It changes colour along the way
There are secretly five chemicals
why: Near the source there is a lot, far away there is hardly any. Cells do different things depending on how much they get, so one chemical can say five different things.
Concentration thresholds. Cells respond to bands of concentration rather than to the exact amount, so a smooth slope is read as a set of discrete regions.

Thresholds plus downstream gene networks that sharpen boundaries by mutual repression. The gradient supplies approximate position; cross-repression between the genes it switches on converts fuzzy edges into crisp ones — which is why real boundaries are far sharper than the gradient that specifies them.

q: What do Hox genes actually do?
What is the function of a Hox gene?
Why does a Hox mutation produce a well-formed structure in the wrong place?
options: They say what kind of thing to build here
They build legs and antennae directly
They control how fast the animal grows
why: They are labels, not builders. The gene says 'this bit is a head' or 'this bit is a middle', and everything else does the building.

They assign identity to a region. The machinery for building a leg exists regardless; the Hox gene decides whether that machinery is the one switched on there. Change the label and you get a correctly built leg in the wrong socket.

Because the addressing and the construction are separate systems. A homeotic mutation misaddresses a fully intact construction programme, which is why the result is a perfect structure in the wrong location rather than a malformed one in the right place. That separation is itself the discovery.

q: Why is the same toolkit in a fly and in a human interesting?
What made the conservation of the developmental toolkit surprising?
options: Because very different animals turn out to be built by the same small set of switches
Because it proves flies and humans are closely related
Because it means all animals develop identically
why: A fly and a person could hardly look less alike. The expectation was that they would need different genes. Instead they use the same small set, switched on in different places and at different times — the difference is in the deployment, not the inventory.

The pre-genomic expectation was that morphological disparity required genetic disparity. What was found instead was a small, highly conserved regulatory toolkit used combinatorially. That relocated the explanation of body-plan difference from gene content to gene regulation, and it is the reason evo-devo exists as a field.

q: Why do you have separate fingers?
How are digits separated during development?
What does interdigital apoptosis illustrate about development?
options: The cells between them were removed on purpose
The fingers grew outwards from a point
They were always separate
why: Your hand started as a paddle with no gaps. The cells in between were told to die, and that is what made the fingers separate.
The limb bud forms as a plate and the interdigital tissue is eliminated by programmed cell death. The fingers are not built apart; the space between them is taken away.

It shows that development is subtractive as well as additive, and that removal is instructed rather than incidental. Where the instruction fails, the digits remain joined — which is exactly what simple syndactyly is.

q: Why can the thread not just be squashed into a ball?
Why is simple compression the wrong solution?
Why is undifferentiated compaction unacceptable?
options: Because it still has to be read, one bit at a time
Because a ball takes up more room
Because DNA is too stiff to squash
why: A tangle would fit. But the cell has to find one small part of it and read it — so it has to be packed in a way that can be undone in one spot without undoing the rest.
Volume is only half the problem. The structure has to permit local, reversible unpacking, because genes are read individually while the rest stays stored.

Compaction and accessibility are competing requirements, and the hierarchical solution satisfies both: each level can be locally relaxed without disturbing the others. A tangle would satisfy the first requirement and destroy the second.

q: When can you actually see a chromosome?
When are chromosomes visible under a light microscope?
Under what condition is a chromosome resolvable by light microscopy?
options: When the cell is dividing and it is packed up tight
All the time
Only when the cell is dead
why: Most of the time the thread is loose so it can be read. It only packs up tight when the cell is about to split, and that is the only time it is thick enough to see.

Chromatin is decondensed during interphase — which is what makes it readable — and condenses only for division. Chromosomes were named and counted for decades before anyone knew what they were made of, precisely because that is the one state visible with the instruments available.

Resolution is the constraint: decondensed chromatin is well below the diffraction limit, and only metaphase condensation brings it above. This is a nice case of a structure being characterised long before its composition, because the observable state was the atypical one.

q: Why is four letters enough?
Why is a four-base alphabet sufficient?
Why is alphabet size the wrong thing to worry about?
options: Because the message is billions of letters long
Because each letter means a lot on its own
Because living things are simple
why: Each extra letter multiplies what you can say by four. Make the message long enough and four letters can say anything.
Capacity grows exponentially with length and only linearly with alphabet size. Three billion positions at four options each is capacity nobody has found a use for all of.

This is why binary is not a limitation for computers either. The alphabet sets bits per symbol — two for DNA — and the length does the rest. The interesting constraints on genomes are error rate and replication cost, not vocabulary.

q: Which letter does C hold hands with?
Which base pairs with cytosine?
What is the complement of cytosine?
options: G
A
T
why: C always goes with G, and A always goes with T. Never any other way round.
C pairs with G, A with T. The rule has no exceptions, and the next lesson is about what that rule makes possible.

C–G, joined by three hydrogen bonds against A–T's two, which is why GC-rich sequence has a higher melting temperature. The pairing is geometric as well as chemical: purine to pyrimidine keeps every rung the same width.

q: How much of a new ladder is brand new?
In a newly replicated double helix, how much is newly synthesised?
What is the composition of a daughter duplex?
options: Half — one side is the original
All of it
None of it
why: Each new ladder is one old side and one new side. That is why it is called semiconservative — half is conserved.
One parental strand and one new one. Meselson and Stahl proved it by weight: after one round every molecule was intermediate in density, which only the semiconservative model predicts.

One parental, one daughter strand. Conservative replication would have given two populations after one round — all-heavy and all-light — and dispersive would never have separated at all. The single intermediate band ruled out both.

q: What is a mutation?
What is a mutation, precisely?
What is the precise definition of a mutation?
options: A letter that got copied wrong and was not fixed
A monster in a film
Something a body does on purpose when it needs to change
why: It is just a copying mistake nobody corrected. Not something the body chose, and usually not dramatic at all.
An uncorrected copying error. Nothing about it is intentional — a cell cannot decide to mutate a gene it would find useful, and this is why the beetles could not simply turn dark.

It is undirected with respect to need, which is the load-bearing part. Bacteria placed under antibiotic pressure do not generate resistance mutations in response to the drug; the variation is present beforehand at low frequency and the drug reveals it. That was the point of the Luria–Delbrück experiment in 1943.

q: Why is a food web safer than a food chain?
Why does a web tolerate a loss that a chain would not?
What property does the chain abstraction discard?
options: If one link goes, there are other routes
Webs have more animals in them
Chains only exist in the sea
why: In a chain, if one thing disappears everything above it goes hungry. In a web there is usually something else to eat, so losing one link does not have to bring the whole thing down.
Redundancy. Multiple routes to the same energy mean the loss of one link can be absorbed — which is why real ecosystems survive losses that a chain diagram predicts would be fatal.

It discards redundancy, which is the property that determines robustness. That makes the chain actively misleading rather than merely simplified: it predicts fragility that is usually absent, and it gives no way to identify the cases — keystone species — where the fragility is real.

q: Why are there so few big predators?
Why is the number of trophic levels limited to four or five?
Why does trophic efficiency bound chain length?
options: There is only a tenth as much energy at each level up
They are killed by people
They breed too slowly
why: Ten thousand units of sunlight becomes about one unit five levels up. There is simply not enough left to feed anything else, so the chain has to stop.
Energy falls by roughly a factor of ten per level, so after four or five levels there is not enough to support a viable population. The limit is arithmetic, not biology.

Each transfer loses about 90%, so available energy falls geometrically while the minimum viable population size does not. The two curves cross after four or five levels, and that crossing is the ceiling. It also explains why top predators need enormous territories — the area required scales with the energy shortfall.

q: What decides how many animals a place can hold?
What sets carrying capacity?
Why does only the scarcest resource matter?
options: Whichever thing they need runs out first
How much space there is
How fast they breed
why: Plenty of grass is no use if there is no water. Whatever they run out of first is what sets the number, and giving them more of anything else makes no difference at all.

The binding constraint, and only that one. Relieving any other requirement changes nothing until the scarce one is relieved too — which is why a single limiting nutrient can control the productivity of a whole system.

Breeding rate determines how fast the ceiling is reached, never how high it is. Confusing the two is why 'they breed too fast' is almost always the wrong diagnosis of an overpopulation problem — the rate sets the approach, the resource sets the level.

q: Why did the plants suffer when the hunters were removed?
Why does removing a predator reduce plant abundance?
Why does the effect alternate in sign as it descends?
options: Nothing was eating the plant eaters any more, so there were far more of them
The hunters had been protecting the plants directly
The plants needed the hunters' waste
why: The hunters never went near the plants. But they kept the plant eaters down — and once they were gone there were more than twice as many mouths, and the plants could not keep up.

Predator release raised herbivore numbers, and the increased grazing pressure suppressed the plants. The route runs through the middle level, which is why the effect is indirect and why nobody expected it.

Because each level suppresses the one below it. Removing a suppressor releases its prey, which suppresses the next level down, so the sign flips at every step. That alternation predicts what happens when you remove a herbivore instead — plants should rise — and it does, which is what makes the account testable.

q: Why does having several species doing the same job help?
What does functional redundancy buy?
Why does redundancy loss produce non-linear failure?
options: If one is lost, another can do it
It makes the ecosystem bigger
They help each other out
why: If only one thing eats a particular plant and it disappears, that job stops. If four things eat it, losing one hardly matters. Spares are what let a web survive losing pieces.

It buys the ability to absorb loss. A role with several occupants continues when one is lost; a role with one occupant does not — and a species in that position is a keystone whether or not it is abundant.

Because redundancy is consumed before function is. Losses are absorbed with no measurable change until the last occupant of some role goes, and then the failure is abrupt. This is why monitoring ecosystem function is a poor early-warning system, and why diversity is worth protecting before anything appears to be wrong.

q: What makes an idea a good one to test?
What makes an idea testable?
Which property makes a claim testable?
Which property makes a claim empirically tractable?
options: It tells you what you should find
Lots of people believe it
It has been around a long time
why: A good idea sticks its neck out. It says: if I am right, you will find THIS. Then you can go and look.
An idea earns its keep by saying in advance what you should find. If it fits whatever you discover, it was never at risk, and an idea that was never at risk has not been tested.

Testability is about forbidden outcomes. A claim that is compatible with every possible observation excludes nothing and so is confirmed by nothing. This is why 'what would change your mind?' is the sharpest question you can ask anyone, including yourself.

A hypothesis is informative in proportion to what it rules out. Popper's asymmetry — that no number of confirmations establishes a universal claim while one clean falsification refutes it — is the strict form; in practice theories are compared on how much they forbid and how well they survive attempts to violate it.

q: Two people look at the same clue and say different things. What helps most?
Two accounts fit the same evidence. What helps you decide between them?
What most effectively discriminates between two accounts that both fit the current evidence?
Given underdetermination by present evidence, what best discriminates two rival accounts?
options: Ask each one what they would expect to find next
See which one sounds more confident
Count how many people agree with each
why: If two people expect different things, go and look. Whoever guessed right has the better idea — and being willing to say what you expect is what makes it a fair test.

Confidence and popularity are not evidence; expectations are. Ask each account what it predicts you will find next, then go and find out. The account that keeps being surprised is in trouble, whichever one it is.

Present evidence usually underdetermines rival accounts, so the discriminating move is forward-looking: derive a novel prediction from each, and test where they diverge. Note that this test is symmetrical — it is only useful if you are willing to apply it to the account you favour.

Novel-prediction success is the standard currency because it is the hardest thing to arrange after the fact. Accommodation of known data is cheap; both rival accounts will manage it. The asymmetry appears only at the points where they forbid different things.

q: What does 'homologous' mean?
What does calling two structures homologous claim?
What is the content of a homology claim?
options: The same parts in the same order, doing different jobs
Two things that do the same job
Two things that look the same from outside
why: It is about the parts underneath, not the job on top. A bat's wing and a bee's wing both fly, but they are not homologous — there are no matching bones, because a bee has none.

Homology is correspondence of parts by position and origin, deliberately defined without reference to function. A bat wing and an insect wing are analogous — same job, no shared parts. A bat wing and a whale flipper are homologous — same parts, no shared job.

The definition is intentionally function-blind, because a function-based definition would make the concept circular. Diagnosis rests on relative position, connectivity and developmental origin, which is why an octopus eye and a vertebrate eye are analogous despite the resemblance: they develop from different tissues and are wired in opposite directions.

q: What is the surprising thing about the fossil layers?
What is the feature of the fossil record that most needs explaining?
Which feature of the record carries the explanatory burden?
options: The order is the same all over the world
There are a lot of fossils
Fossils are made of stone
why: Fossils being common is not surprising. The same order turning up on every continent is — that is a pattern, and patterns need a reason.
Abundance is unremarkable; consistency of sequence across independent sites is not. A pattern that could easily have come out otherwise and did not is the thing an account has to earn.

Global consistency of relative order is the explanandum, because it is highly specific and would have been easy to violate. Both accounts on offer are attempts to supply a sorting mechanism for it, and both should be judged on how much they forbid.

q: Why do scientists care more about shared mistakes than shared working parts?
Why is a shared defect treated as stronger evidence than a shared function?
Why does a shared inactivating lesion carry more inferential weight than shared function?
options: Because there are far more ways to break something than to make it work
Because broken things are more interesting
Because working parts are harder to compare
why: Two people can spell a word right for the same reason: it is right. Spelling it wrong the same way needs an explanation.

Function constrains: there may be only a few ways to build a working enzyme, so independent arrival at the same solution is unremarkable. Failure does not constrain — the space of possible breaks is huge, so a shared specific break is a much narrower coincidence.

It is an argument from the size of the outcome space. Convergence on function is expected under constraint; convergence on one particular lesion out of an enormous set of equally-disabling alternatives is not. This is why the argument targets shared derived defects specifically, and why demonstrating function in the sequence is the relevant counter-move.

q: What do both sides of this argument actually agree about?
Which of these is agreed by both accounts?
Which claim is common ground across the dispute?
options: That natural selection is real and new species appear
That nothing ever changes
That all life shares one ancestor
why: Natural selection is not the argument. Both sides think it happens. The argument is about how far it can take you.
Selection, mutation and speciation are common ground. Finding the actual point of disagreement — the ceiling — is what makes it possible to argue about the right thing.

Locating the genuine locus of dispute is a discipline worth having in every argument, not only this one. Most heat here is generated by attacking positions the other side does not hold: selection and speciation are accepted on both accounts, and universal common descent is the contested claim.

q: What makes a gene a gene?
What defines the boundaries of a gene?
What individuates a gene?
options: It has a start, a stop, and something it makes
It is a fixed number of letters long
It is the part of DNA that is coloured differently
why: Genes are all different lengths. What they share is a signal saying where to start reading, a signal saying where to stop, and something they make.
Boundaries and product, not size. Genes vary from a few hundred bases to over two million, so length tells you nothing about whether you are looking at one.

The individuation is functional and regulatory rather than structural, which is exactly why the concept frays at the edges: overlapping reading frames, nested genes and alternative splicing all break the assumption that the genome partitions cleanly into units.

q: Is the instruction the same thing as the eye?
What is the relationship between a gene and the trait it affects?
How does genotype relate to phenotype?
options: No — one is the recipe, the other is what gets made
Yes, they are the same thing
The gene is a tiny copy of the eye
why: The recipe is not the cake. A gene is instructions for making something, and lots of other things affect how it turns out.
The sequence you carry is your genotype; what you actually end up with is your phenotype. Food, temperature, chance and other genes all sit between them.

The mapping is many-to-many and heavily context-dependent. Identical twins share a genotype and are distinguishable, which is the cleanest everyday demonstration that the relation is not identity — and the reason 'a gene for X' is nearly always a misleading phrase.

q: What is different between a liver cell and a nerve cell?
What differs between two cell types in the same body?
What is the locus of difference between differentiated cell types?
options: Which genes they are reading
Which genes they have
How many chromosomes they have
why: They both have all the instructions. They are just reading different bits — and the bits they are not reading are still there.
The genome is identical; the expression pattern is not. This is why a skin cell can be reprogrammed back into something that can become anything — nothing was ever thrown away.

Difference is regulatory, not genomic. The strongest evidence is reversibility: somatic cell nuclear transfer produces a whole organism from a differentiated nucleus, which would be impossible if differentiation involved loss.

q: Why is a dominant copy dominant?
Why is a dominant allele dominant?
What is the usual mechanistic basis of dominance?
options: Because one working copy makes enough
Because it is stronger than the other one
Because it comes from the father
why: Nothing is fighting anything. If one copy makes enough of what you need, having a broken second copy does not show.

It is a dosage fact, not a contest. One functional allele generally produces sufficient product, so the broken one is invisible — which also explains why some conditions are not recessive: where half the normal amount is not enough, one broken copy does show.

Dominance is a consequence of the shape of the dose-response curve. Most enzymes operate well above the level at which output limits flux, so halving them changes nothing measurable. Where flux is dose-sensitive you get haploinsufficiency instead, and the same class of mutation becomes dominant.

q: Did the trait really skip a generation?
In what sense did the trait skip a generation?
Is 'skipping a generation' an accurate description?
options: No — the instruction was there, it just did not show
Yes, it was gone and came back
Yes, it jumped from grandmother to grandchild directly
why: Your mother had the broken copy and passed it to you. She had a working copy too, so it never showed in her.
The allele was transmitted at every step. Only the phenotype was absent, because the intervening carrier also had a working copy. Nothing skipped anything.

Genotype and phenotype come apart here, which is precisely why the distinction is worth having. Nothing can jump a generation — transmission is strictly stepwise — so any apparent skip is an unexpressed carrier.

q: Who tells all your cells what to do?
What coordinates the cells of a body?
How is coordination achieved without central control?
options: Nobody — each reacts to what is around it
The brain, cell by cell
The heart
why: No cell is in charge and no cell can see the whole body. Each one just responds to the chemicals and cells right next to it, and the whole thing works out.

Coordination is local and chemical. A cell responds to what touches it and to signals reaching it; there is no address book and no central instruction. Your brain has no connection at all to most of your cells.

It is distributed control with no controller — the same class of system as the beetle population, and the same reason it is counter-intuitive. Order at the top does not require an orderer, only rules at the bottom and a lot of iterations.

q: Why can your body not just let things spread on their own?
Why is diffusion insufficient for a body your size?
Why does body size force the evolution of circulation?
options: Diffusion is fine over tiny distances and hopeless over big ones
Diffusion only works in water
Diffusion stops working once you are born
why: Diffusion is quick across a cell and impossibly slow across a body. Over a centimetre it would take hours, and you would be dead long before the oxygen arrived.

Diffusion time rises with the square of distance. Crossing a cell takes under a millisecond; crossing a centimetre of tissue would take hours. Circulation exists to carry things the long way quickly, so diffusion only ever has to cover the last few micrometres.

The t ∝ x² scaling is the whole argument, and it is why every animal above a millimetre or so has some form of bulk transport. It also explains capillary density: the system's job is to get a vessel within diffusion distance of every cell, which is why no cell in you sits more than about 20 micrometres from one.

q: What makes oxygen go into your blood?
What drives oxygen across the alveolar wall?
What accounts for net oxygen flux into the pulmonary capillary?
options: There is more of it in the air than in the blood
The lungs suck it in
The blood grabs hold of it
why: It is exactly what you watched in the membrane. More outside than inside means more happens to wander in than out. Nothing pulls it.

A concentration difference plus random motion. Breathing keeps fresh air arriving so the gradient stays steep, and blood flow keeps carrying the oxygen away — but the crossing itself is unassisted diffusion.

Net flux is proportional to the partial pressure gradient, and both ventilation and perfusion exist to maintain that gradient rather than to move the gas. Haemoglobin sharpens it further by binding oxygen and so keeping dissolved concentration low, which steepens the gradient it is diffusing down.

q: What actually crosses into you?
What is absorbed across the gut wall?
What is the absorbed form, and why that form?
options: Small pieces: sugars, amino acids, fatty acids
The food itself, in small lumps
Only water and salt
why: Big things cannot cross the wall, and anyway they are built to somebody else's plan. You take them apart into the standard pieces and build your own.
Monomers cross, polymers do not. That solves two problems at once — size, which the membrane lesson covered, and specification, since a cow's protein is the wrong protein for you regardless.

Reduction to monomers is what makes any food substitutable for any other. It is also why the process must be thorough: an intact protein crossing the barrier is precisely the signal the immune system treats as foreign, which is the basis of food allergy.

q: Why does the loop need a signal coming back?
Why is the return path essential rather than a refinement?
Why does open-loop control fail here specifically?
options: So it knows when to stop and does not overshoot
So the brain can keep a record
So it can happen twice
why: Without something reporting back, the response has no way of knowing the problem is fixed. It keeps pushing, overshoots, and then has to correct the other way.

Feedback is what makes the response proportional to the remaining error. Without it the effector runs at full output regardless, so the system overshoots and oscillates rather than settling — instability, not just imprecision.

The controlled variable is the same one being sensed, which is what closes the loop and makes the correction self-limiting. Open loop, the output is independent of the result, so any disturbance or drift accumulates. Baroreflex failure produces exactly this clinically: pressure that swings wildly rather than pressure that is simply low.

q: Does your skin know what it is keeping out?
Do innate defences identify what they are stopping?
On what basis does innate immunity discriminate?
options: No — it stops everything the same way
Yes, it recognises each germ
Only if you have met that germ before
why: Skin does not identify anything. It is a wall, and a wall works on whatever arrives. That is why it is so effective and why a burn or a cut is so dangerous.

Innate defences are non-specific. They act on broad features rather than identities, which is what lets them respond in minutes — and why breaching them, by a wound or a catheter, is such a common route to serious infection.

Pattern recognition rather than identification: receptors for conserved molecular features that pathogens cannot easily discard. This is the trade the system makes — speed and breadth for precision — and it is why the adaptive system exists to cover what gets through.

q: Were the right cells made because the germ arrived?
Are matching lymphocytes produced in response to the antigen?
In what sense is the antigen not instructive?
options: No — they were already there, and the germ picked them out
Yes, the body designs a cell to fit each germ
Yes, the germ teaches the cells what shape to be
why: The cells with the right shape were made at random, before the germ ever arrived. All the germ did was find them — and then they copied themselves.

The repertoire is generated in advance and randomly. Antigen selects from what already exists; it does not instruct anything to change. This is exactly the distinction you drew about antibiotic resistance, in a different system.

The instructive theory — antigen acting as a template for antibody shape — was the leading account into the 1950s and was displaced by clonal selection. The decisive consideration was the same one that settles the resistance question: the specificity exists before the encounter, and the encounter only amplifies it.

q: Does a vaccine kill germs?
Is a vaccine a treatment?
Why is calling a vaccine a medicine a category error?
options: No — it teaches your body to, before you meet any
Yes, that is what is in it
Yes, but only weakly
why: There is nothing in a vaccine that kills anything. It shows your body a shape, and your body gets ready. All the killing is done by you, later.

A vaccine contains no antimicrobial agent and treats no existing illness. It supplies an antigen so that clonal selection happens in advance, which is why it must be given before exposure to be useful.

Medicines act on a disease process; a vaccine acts on the immune system before there is any disease process. The distinction matters practically: it explains why vaccines are given to well people, why timing is everything, and why 'does it cure it?' is the wrong question to evaluate one by.

q: Why does vaccinating you protect someone who cannot be vaccinated?
How does individual vaccination confer population-level protection?
options: Because a germ that cannot find a susceptible host stops spreading
Because immunity passes between people
Because it makes the germ weaker
why: Nothing passes from you to them. But a germ needs to keep finding people it can infect, and if enough people around it cannot be infected, the chain of transmission breaks before it reaches the person who is vulnerable.

Transmission requires each infection to produce at least one more. Raising the immune fraction reduces the effective reproduction number; once it falls below one, chains die out and the unvaccinated are protected by the absence of transmission rather than by any immunity of their own. This is why the threshold is a function of R₀ — around 95% for measles — and why coverage falling a few points can restore epidemics that were absent for decades.

q: Why does your body make cells that attack you at all?
Why are self-reactive lymphocytes produced in the first place?
Why is self-reactivity unavoidable given the mechanism?
options: Because the shapes are random, and random includes you
Because it is a mistake that should not happen
Because you have been infected by something
why: The shapes are made at random so that some of them will fit germs nobody has met. Random means random — some of them fit you instead. There is no way to have one without the other.

Randomness is what gives the repertoire its coverage, and randomness cannot be selective about what it happens to match. Self-reactive cells are a necessary by-product, which is why an entire screening organ exists to remove them.

It is a structural consequence, not an error. Any system generating specificity without prior knowledge of its targets must generate self-reactivity, and must therefore also implement a separate deletion step. The thymus is the cost of the strategy.

q: Why did nobody know about germs until 350 years ago?
Why was microbial life undiscovered for the whole of recorded history?
What made microbial life inaccessible before the 1670s?
options: They are far too small to see without a lens
There were fewer of them then
Nobody thought to look
why: They were everywhere the whole time. Nobody could see them, and you cannot investigate something you have no way of detecting.

It was an instrument problem, not a curiosity problem. People had wondered about invisible causes of disease for centuries; what was missing was any way to look, and a good enough lens supplied it immediately.

The observation was gated entirely on optics, which is why the discovery arrives so suddenly and so completely once lens-making improves. It is a clean example of a whole domain of nature being inaccessible not for want of thought but for want of an instrument — and a reason to be careful about concluding that something does not exist.

q: Why do bacteria evolve so much faster than animals?
Why is evolutionary change so rapid in bacteria?
What makes generation time the rate-limiter on adaptation?
options: They have a new generation every twenty minutes
Their DNA is less accurate
They want to change more
why: Selection needs generations to work with. A bacterium has three an hour, so what would take an elephant a thousand years takes a germ a fortnight.
The three conditions act once per generation, so the number of generations sets the pace. Twenty minutes against twenty years is a factor of half a million, and that is nearly the whole explanation.

Population size compounds it: a culture holds enough individuals that even very rare mutations are present somewhere, so a bacterial population explores sequence space vastly faster than a large-bodied animal can. Rate and number, not any difference in the mechanism.

q: Are the bacteria living in you a bad thing?
Is the resident microbiota harmful, harmless or necessary?
In what sense is the microbiome functionally part of the organism?
options: No — you need them, and you are unhealthy without them
Yes, all bacteria cause illness
They make no difference either way
why: They do jobs you cannot do yourself: getting energy out of food you cannot digest, making vitamins you cannot make, and teaching your defences what to leave alone.

They are necessary. Germ-free animals are demonstrably abnormal — poorly developed guts, miscalibrated immune systems — which establishes that the community is doing work the host depends on rather than merely tolerating it.

It supplies metabolic capability absent from the host genome and participates in host development, which is a functional rather than a rhetorical sense of 'part of'. It is also why broad-spectrum antibiotics have consequences beyond the infection they treat: they are not selective about which community members they remove.

q: Why does one spot mean one cell?
Why does a colony correspond to a single founding cell?
Why does the method depend on adequate dilution?
options: The spot is all the descendants of one cell that landed there
Bacteria always arrive in groups of one
The spots are drawn on afterwards
why: A single cell lands, and cannot move. It divides where it is until there are millions of copies in a heap you can see. So one spot means one cell arrived there.

Bacteria on a solid surface are effectively immobile, so all descendants of one cell stay in one place and form a visible clone. Dilution matters because the correspondence only holds if cells land far enough apart to grow into separate colonies.

The one-cell-one-colony correspondence is the entire basis of the count, and it breaks when colonies merge. This is why plates are counted only in a specific range — typically 30 to 300 — with anything denser being reported as too numerous to count rather than estimated.

q: Did any single beetle change colour?
Did any individual beetle change during the simulation?
What exactly changed over the generations?
At which level did the change occur?
options: No — only which beetles were left changed
Yes, each beetle got slowly darker
Yes, the babies chose to be darker
why: Every beetle kept the colour it hatched with. What changed was who was still there to have babies — and their babies looked like them.
No individual changed. Each beetle kept its shade for life. The population's average moved because the mismatched ones were eaten before breeding, and offspring resembled the survivors.

The individual is not the unit that changes. Each beetle's shade was fixed at hatching; the distribution moved because survival was not independent of shade. Change at the population level with none at the individual level is the signature of selection.

Selection acts on individuals and changes populations. Confusing the two levels produces Lamarckian intuitions — the beetle striving and darkening — which the simulation rules out by construction: shade is assigned at hatching and never written to again.

q: You switched off 'babies like parents' and it stopped. Why?
Removing heredity halted adaptation even though the predator still ate the mismatched beetles. Why?
Why does removing heritability halt adaptation, given that differential mortality still occurs?
options: The killing still happened, but nothing was passed on, so each generation started over
The bird stopped being able to see them
Fewer beetles died once heredity was off
why: Exactly the same beetles got eaten. But their babies came out any colour at all, so the next round began from scratch. Selection with nothing inherited is just killing.

Mortality was unchanged — the same mismatched beetles died. But offspring shade was drawn independently of the parents, so the survivors' advantage was not transmitted. Each generation restarted from the same distribution.

Differential mortality without transmission produces no cumulative change. Selection sorts a generation; heredity is what makes the sorting persist. Remove it and each generation is an independent sample — the population is culled every round and returns to the same mean every round.

q: Where can you actually watch this happen?
Which of these is natural selection you can observe directly?
Which of these is a directly observed instance of natural selection?
Which is an observation rather than an inference about the unobserved past?
options: Germs becoming hard to kill with medicine
Only in books about long ago
Nowhere — it is too slow to see
why: You can watch it in a week in a dish of germs. It is not a story about long ago — it is happening in hospitals right now.
Antibiotic resistance is measured in laboratories in days and in hospitals in weeks. So is pesticide resistance in insects, and so is the peppered moth, which was counted year by year.

Selection is observational science: resistance evolution is measured in real time, the peppered moth was censused across decades, and Darwin's finches have been tracked bird by bird on Daphne Major since 1973. None of these requires an inference about the deep past.

This matters for how the claim is classified. Variation, heritability and differential survival are each independently measurable, and their joint consequence has been observed repeatedly under controlled conditions. Whatever one concludes about the history of life, this mechanism is not in dispute — it is demonstrated.

q: Can an animal be fit and unfit at the same time?
Can one organism have two different fitnesses?
In what sense is fitness not a property of an organism?
options: Yes — in two different places
No, fitness is fixed at birth
Only if it moves house
why: Fitness is not a thing an animal has, like weight. It is about how well it does where it actually is, so the same animal has a different answer in a different place.
Fitness is a relation between an organism and an environment, so one organism has as many fitnesses as there are environments to put it in. Nothing about the animal has to change for the number to.

This is why 'the environment selects' is a better formulation than 'the fittest survive'. It also explains heterozygote advantage: the sickle-cell allele is a liability where there is no malaria and an asset where there is, so selection maintains it at intermediate frequency in exactly the places malaria is endemic.

q: A population changes over time. Is that always selection?
Does directional change in a population entail selection?
options: No — it can drift by chance, especially if the population is small
Yes, change always means selection
Only if the change is large
why: You saw this in the simulation: with the predator picking at random the line still wandered, and sometimes it wandered the right way. Change happened, and nothing was being selected.

Sampling error alone moves allele frequencies, and it does so faster in small populations. Distinguishing drift from selection is a real statistical problem, not a technicality — it is why 'the population changed' and 'the population adapted' are two different claims, and why demonstrating selection requires more than showing a trend.

q: Does the medicine make the germs resistant?
Does antibiotic exposure cause resistance mutations?
What did Luria and Delbrück's variance argument establish?
options: No — it kills the ones that were not, and the rest breed
Yes, it teaches them to resist
Yes, it damages their DNA and they change
why: The germs that could survive were already there before the medicine arrived. All the medicine did was clear away the competition.
Resistance is not induced. Some bacteria already carried it, at low frequency, and the drug removed everything else — leaving them the entire population to grow into.

That mutations arise independently of selection. The fluctuation test compared observed variance in resistant counts against what an induced response would predict; the observed variance was far too high, which is only explicable if mutations occurred before exposure, at random times during growth.

q: How does your brain know something hurt a lot?
How is stimulus intensity encoded if amplitude is fixed?
What channels remain for intensity once amplitude is unavailable?
options: Lots of signals arrive, quickly
The signals are bigger
The signals travel faster
why: Every signal is the same size, so size cannot tell you anything. What changes is how many arrive and how fast they come — a hard press sends a flood, a light touch sends a trickle.
Rate and recruitment. A stronger stimulus fires each neuron more often and brings more neurons above threshold; amplitude is fixed and carries nothing.

Frequency and population coding, and they are what is left rather than what was chosen. The all-or-nothing law removes amplitude as a variable, so any information about intensity must be carried by the remaining degrees of freedom.

q: Why is a gap better than a wire here?
What does a chemical synapse buy over a direct electrical connection?
Why is the conversion to chemical and back worth its cost in speed?
options: It can be made stronger or weaker, so the brain can learn
Chemicals travel faster than electricity
It stops the cells getting tangled
why: A wire is always the same. A gap can be made easier or harder to cross — and changing how easy each gap is to cross is what learning actually is inside your head.
Adjustability. Transmitter released, receptor number and clearance rate can all change with use, so the connection has a strength that experience can set. A direct electrical junction is fixed.

It costs perhaps half a millisecond and buys plasticity, inhibition and signal inversion. Electrical synapses do exist and are faster — they are used where speed matters more than modifiability, such as escape reflexes — which is the clearest evidence that the chemical one is a deliberate trade rather than a limitation.

q: Is what you see the same as what is there?
What is the relationship between the retinal image and what you perceive?
In what sense is perception inferential rather than receptive?
options: No — it is your brain's best guess from what arrives
Yes, your eyes send a picture to your brain
Yes, unless you have something wrong with your eyes
why: Your eyes do not send a picture. They send patches of information with holes in it, and your brain builds something complete out of that. You just showed yourself one of the holes.

The image is incomplete, and what you experience is a reconstruction. You demonstrated the point yourself: the thumb vanished and background appeared, which means something manufactured that background.

The mapping from scene to retinal image loses information irreversibly, so recovering the scene is underdetermined and requires assumptions. Perception is the output of that inference. Illusions are not malfunctions — they are the inference machinery running correctly on input it was not built for.

q: Why does telling a story often make it less accurate?
Why does rehearsal reduce a memory's fidelity while increasing confidence?
Why do confidence and accuracy come apart with rehearsal?
options: Each telling rebuilds it, and the rebuilt version is what gets kept
Because people exaggerate on purpose
Because memories fade with time
why: Nobody is lying. Every time you tell it you build it again out of pieces, and any small change you make gets saved as the new version. Tell it fifty times and you are remembering the fiftieth telling.

Each retrieval destabilises and re-stores the trace, so alterations persist. Fluency rises with practice and fluency feels like accuracy — which is why the most-rehearsed account is both the most confident and the most drifted.

They are tracking different things. Confidence tracks ease of retrieval, which rehearsal reliably improves; accuracy tracks correspondence to the event, which rehearsal can only degrade. Nothing in the system measures the second, so there is no internal signal that would tell you.

q: Was your brain in charge of pulling your hand away?
Is the withdrawal reflex directed by the brain?
What is the brain's role in a spinal reflex?
options: No — the spinal cord decided, and your brain was told afterwards
Yes, it decided very quickly
Yes, but subconsciously
why: The decision was made in your spinal cord, where the message turned straight round. The signal to your brain went off at the same time and arrived later, which is why the movement comes before the pain.
The arc is complete within the cord. The ascending pathway runs in parallel and produces the sensation afterwards — the ordering you notice is real and it is a consequence of the wiring.
The brain is informed, not consulted. It can modulate the reflex — you can suppress withdrawal deliberately, up to a point — but the loop closes without it, and that is what the architecture is for.

q: What is a tree mostly made of?
What is the source of the carbon in wood?
Where does the carbon in a tree's dry mass originate?
options: Carbon that used to be in the air
Minerals it pulled up from the soil
Water it soaked up through its roots
why: Every bit of wood is built from carbon dioxide the tree took out of the air. The soil gives it a few minerals and holds it upright, and that is nearly all.

Wood is roughly half carbon by dry mass, and all of that carbon entered as atmospheric CO₂. Soil contributes minerals in trace quantities — which is why a hydroponically grown plant does perfectly well with no soil at all.

The soil supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and trace elements in small amounts; the bulk is atmospheric carbon fixed by the Calvin cycle. This is also why afforestation is a carbon sink in a literal rather than metaphorical sense — the carbon is structurally in the tree.

q: What actually moves the water up?
What provides the motive force?
Where does the energy for lifting come from?
options: Evaporation at the top, pulling the thread behind it
The roots pumping it up
The stem squeezing rhythmically
why: Nothing pushes. Water leaves the leaves, and because water molecules hold onto each other, the ones behind get dragged along — all the way down to the roots.

The energy is the sun's, spent evaporating water from the leaf surface. The column is pulled from above rather than pushed from below, which is why height is not limited the way a pump would limit it.

The plant contributes no metabolic energy to the lifting at all — evaporation is driven by the atmosphere's water potential. Root pressure exists and is real, but it is a minor contribution and cannot account for anything like the observed heights.

q: Why does a plant not just keep its holes wide open?
Why is maximum aperture not optimal?
Why does the marginal value of aperture fall to zero while its cost does not?
options: It would run out of water before the day was over
It would get too much carbon dioxide
The holes would break
why: You watched it happen. Wide open makes sugar fast and empties the leaf of water, and a dead leaf makes no sugar at all. The most it can do is not the best it can do.

Transpirational loss rises with aperture without limit, while sugar production stops rising once light rather than CO₂ is limiting. Past that point the leaf pays more and gains nothing — and if loss exceeds root supply for long enough it dies, having produced less than a more modest setting would have.

Photosynthesis saturates and transpiration does not. That asymmetry is what makes an intermediate optimal, and because the position of the optimum depends on humidity, wind and temperature, it has to be tracked rather than set — which is what guard cells are for.

q: Why is a bird-pollinated flower red and unscented?
Why do bird-pollinated flowers converge on red with little scent?
What does the red-and-scentless combination tell you about the receiver?
options: Birds see red well and smell poorly; bees are the opposite
Red is the strongest colour
Scent would attract the wrong birds
why: Birds see red very well and hardly smell at all, so a red flower with no scent is shouting at birds and staying invisible to bees. It is advertising to one customer and nobody else.

The signal is matched to the receiver's sensory system. Red is outside useful bee vision and well within bird vision, and scent would be wasted on an animal that barely smells. Excluding the wrong visitor matters as much as attracting the right one, because pollen given to the wrong courier is lost.

It is evidence read backwards: the flower's advertisement tells you what its intended customer can perceive. Convergence on the same combination across unrelated plant families on different continents is the strongest form of that argument — the same receiver produces the same signal wherever the relationship arises.

q: What problem is a flower solving?
What constraint does the flower exist to overcome?
Why is reproduction the hardest problem for a sessile organism?
options: The plant cannot move, but its pollen has to
Attracting sunlight to the plant
Keeping insects away from the leaves
why: A plant is stuck where it grew. Its pollen still has to get to a different plant, so it pays an animal to carry it — that is what the colour and the nectar are for.

Gametes must reach another individual and the individual cannot travel. The flower solves it by recruiting something that can, paying in nectar, and shaping itself so the payment cannot be collected without the service being done.

Because it is the one function that cannot be performed locally. Feeding, drinking and defending can all be done in place; outcrossing cannot, so it must be delegated — to an animal, or to the wind, and both routes shape the flower entirely.

q: What told the string what shape to be?
Where is the information for the fold stored?
In what sense does the sequence encode the structure?
options: Nothing did — the shape is what the order of beads makes happen
A folding machine in the cell
The shape is written down in the DNA separately
why: Nobody folds it. Put those beads in that order in water and that shape is what you get, because it is the arrangement the beads settle into.
There is no separate instruction for shape. The DNA specifies the order of amino acids and nothing else; the structure is a consequence of that order plus water.

The encoding is implicit rather than explicit. The genome stores a one-dimensional string and the three-dimensional structure is computed by physics at run time — which is precisely why predicting structure from sequence was an unsolved problem for fifty years.

q: You unfold a protein but break nothing. Does it still work?
An unfolded protein retains every bond. Is it functional?
Why does denaturation abolish function without altering composition?
options: No — the shape was the job
Yes, all the parts are still there
Only if it was a small protein
why: Nothing has been taken away. But the working part of a protein is the shape of its surface, and once that is gone there is nothing left to do the job.
Every atom and every covalent bond is intact. Function lived in the arrangement — the pocket, the surface, the geometry — and unfolding destroys that while leaving the chemistry untouched.

The catalytic or binding site is an emergent property of the tertiary structure: residues far apart in sequence are brought together in space to form it. Unfolding separates them, and the site simply ceases to exist as a feature.

q: Why does an enzyme only do one job?
What is the basis of enzyme specificity?
Why are specificity and catalysis inseparable?
options: Because only one shape fits its notch
Because it is programmed to
Because it only meets one kind of molecule
why: The notch is a particular shape. Only a molecule that matches it can get in, so that is the only reaction it can help with.

The active site's geometry is what positions a substrate correctly, and a pocket shaped to fit one molecule precisely cannot fit another. Specificity is not a separate feature — it is the same feature.

Catalytic power comes from complementarity to the transition state, and complementarity is by definition exclusive. An enzyme that accepted many substrates would position none of them well enough to accelerate anything, so promiscuity and efficiency trade off directly.

q: Why does activity fall above the optimum temperature?
Why is the fall in activity above the optimum not simply the reverse of the rise?
options: The enzyme is unfolding, and that does not reverse on cooling
The reaction runs out of substrate
The molecules move too fast to collide
why: Below the peak, more heat means more collisions and more reaction. Above it, the heat is shaking the protein apart — and once it has unfolded and stuck to its neighbours, cooling it down does not bring it back.

The two effects are asymmetric in kind. Collision frequency is a smooth reversible function of temperature; denaturation is a cooperative transition that destroys the active site and is usually followed by irreversible aggregation. That asymmetry is why the curve is not a symmetric peak, and why a fever above about 42 °C is dangerous rather than merely uncomfortable.

q: Why is a sticky misfolded protein dangerous?
Why does misfolding cause disease beyond the loss of function?
What makes amyloid pathology self-propagating?
options: It makes others fold wrong too, and they pile up
It stops the cell making new proteins
It uses up all the water
why: The wrong shape has sticky bits on the outside. It grabs others, they clump, and the clumps get bigger — losing one protein would not matter much, but a growing pile does.

The misfolded form templates the same misfolding in normal copies, so the problem grows rather than staying constant, and the aggregates themselves are toxic. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and type 2 diabetes all involve protein aggregation.

Amyloid is a cross-β structure that is thermodynamically very stable and grows by recruiting monomers onto its ends. That is self-templating — which is why prion diseases are transmissible without any nucleic acid at all, a claim that took Prusiner a decade to get accepted.

q: What makes something alive?
What distinguishes living from non-living matter?
On what does the living/non-living distinction rest?
options: What it does and keeps doing
A special sort of stuff inside it
Whether it can move about
why: There is no special living material. Everything in you is the same kind of stuff as a rock — it is what it is all doing together that makes the difference.
No component is distinctive; the organisation is. Living things maintain themselves against decay, and that maintenance is the thing being pointed at, not any ingredient.

Movement is a poor criterion — a tree does not move and is alive, a river does and is not. The property that does the work is self-maintenance: living systems expend energy to hold themselves away from equilibrium, and stop being alive precisely when they stop.

q: A tree cannot walk. Is it alive?
A tree does not move from its position. Does that count against it being alive?
How should a single failed criterion be weighed?
options: Yes — it does nearly all the others
No, moving is required
Only partly alive
why: Missing one sign does not matter much. A tree grows, uses energy, senses light, gets rid of waste and makes seeds — that is plenty.
One failure carries almost no weight in a cluster concept. A tree satisfies six of seven comfortably, and moving turns out to be the least important of them.

Weight it as evidence rather than as a gate. This is why 'is a virus alive?' has no clean answer and does not need one — the useful question is which properties it has and which it lacks, and that question does have an answer.

q: Why is a fire not alive?
What does a flame fundamentally lack?
Which two properties does combustion lack?
options: It carries no instructions and captures no energy
It is not made of cells
It cannot move on its own
why: A fire does lots of things living things do. But it has no recipe for itself, and it throws all its energy away as heat instead of using it.
No heredity and no coupling. A new flame inherits nothing from the old one, so nothing can accumulate; and the energy leaves as heat rather than being captured to do work.

Both are needed and neither is present. Without energy capture there is nothing to power maintenance; without heredity there is nothing to select on, so a fire cannot adapt in any generation, however many flames it lights.

q: Has anyone ever made something alive out of things that were not alive?
What is the current experimental status of the origin of life?
What is the honest experimental status of abiogenesis?
options: No. Some of the steps, but not the whole thing
Yes, in 1953
Yes, it happens in laboratories all the time
why: The famous experiment made building blocks, not a living thing. It is still an open question, and anyone who tells you it is settled is going beyond the evidence.
Individual steps have been achieved; the whole has not. Both sides of the disagreement accept this, and a textbook or a video that implies otherwise has overstated the case.

This is worth being precise about, because it is misreported in both directions: popular accounts sometimes imply the problem is solved, and some critiques imply no progress has been made. Neither is accurate. Substantial partial results exist; a complete route does not.
